content.snl: Set.statement(%Set theory is the mathematical study of sets, which are abstract collections of objects. It serves as a foundational framework for nearly all of modern mathematics.%)
Set.statement(%We introduce the fundamental notions of set theory: sets, elements, equality, subsets, and the power set.%)

Set.statement(%A set is a collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right. The objects in a set are called its elements or members. We typically denote sets by capital letters %, $A, B, C, \ldots$, % and elements by lowercase letters %, $x, y, z, \ldots$, %.%)
Set.statement(%Let %, $A$, % be a set and %, $x$, % an object. We write %, Set.in($x$, $A$), % if %, $x$, % is an element of %, $A$, %, and %, Set.notin($x$, $A$), % otherwise.%)
Set.statement(%There exists a unique set containing no elements, called the empty set and denoted %, Set.emptyset, %. For any object %, $x$, %, we have %, Set.notin($x$, Set.emptyset), %.%)

Set.statement(%Two sets %, $A$, % and %, $B$, % are equal, denoted %, $A = B$, %, if and only if they have exactly the same elements. Formally, %, $A = B \iff (\forall x)($, Set.in($x$, $A$), $\iff$, Set.in($x$, $B$), $)$, %. This axiom captures the principle that a set is completely determined by its elements.%)

Set.statement(%Let %, $A$, % and %, $B$, % be sets. We say %, $A$, % is a subset of %, $B$, %, denoted %, Set.subset($A$, $B$), %, if every element of %, $A$, % is also an element of %, $B$, %. Formally, %, Set.subset($A$, $B$), % means %, $(\forall x)($, Set.in($x$, $A$), $\implies$, Set.in($x$, $B$), $)$, %. We also say %, $B$, % is a superset of %, $A$, %, denoted %, Set.supset($B$, $A$), %.%)

Set.statement(%Let %, $A$, % and %, $B$, % be sets. We say %, $A$, % is a proper subset of %, $B$, %, denoted %, Set.subsetneq($A$, $B$), %, if %, Set.subset($A$, $B$), % and %, $A \neq B$, %. That is, every element of %, $A$, % is in %, $B$, %, but there exists at least one element of %, $B$, % that is not in %, $A$, %.%)

Set.statement(%The power set of a set %, $A$, %, denoted %, Set.powerset($A$), %, is the set of all subsets of %, $A$, %. Formally, %, Set.powerset($A$), $= \{\, B \mid$, Set.subset($B$, $A$), $\,\}$, %. Note that %, Set.in(Set.emptyset, Set.powerset($A$)), % and %, Set.in($A$, Set.powerset($A$)), % for any set %, $A$, %.%)
Set.statement(%We define the basic operations on sets: union, intersection, and set difference.%)

Set.statement(%Let %, $A$, % and %, $B$, % be sets. Their union, denoted %, Set.cup($A$, $B$), %, is the set of all elements that belong to %, $A$, %, to %, $B$, %, or to both. Formally, %, Set.cup($A$, $B$), $= \{\, x \mid$, Set.in($x$, $A$), $\text{ or }$, Set.in($x$, $B$), $\,\}$, %.%)

Set.statement(%Let %, $A$, % and %, $B$, % be sets. Their intersection, denoted %, Set.cap($A$, $B$), %, is the set of all elements that belong to both %, $A$, % and %, $B$, %. Formally, %, Set.cap($A$, $B$), $= \{\, x \mid$, Set.in($x$, $A$), $\text{ and }$, Set.in($x$, $B$), $\,\}$, %. Two sets are called disjoint if %, Set.cap($A$, $B$), $=$, Set.emptyset, %.%)

Set.statement(%Let %, $A$, % and %, $B$, % be sets. The set difference %, Set.setminus($A$, $B$), % is the set of all elements of %, $A$, % that are not elements of %, $B$, %. Formally, %, Set.setminus($A$, $B$), $= \{\, x \in$, $A$, $\mid$, Set.notin($x$, $B$), $\,\}$, %. Note that %, Set.setminus($A$, $B$), % is generally different from %, Set.setminus($B$, $A$), %.%)
